newsitem.title: JAPAN: China warns against enlarged U.S.-Japan alliance.
newsitem.headline: China warns against enlarged U.S.-Japan alliance.

text.p: Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang warned Japan on Monday not to enlarge the scope of its security alliance with the United States and said Beijing wanted to start talks with Tokyo over a thorny islands dispute.
"The objective of the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty is to defend the security of Japan," Shen told a news conference in Tokyo. "If it moves out of this framework, it will raise concerns in Asia."
Shen, who arrived in Japan on Sunday on a nine-day visit, also said Japan and China must resolve the dispute over a group of uninhabited islands in the East China Sea through dialogue.
"We must try to understand and respect each other," Shen said of the dispute over the islands, called the Senkakus in Japan and the Diaoyus in China.
"This issue must be resolved from the point of view of the whole of Sino-Japanese relations," Shen said. "We wish to start such talks some time in the future."
Last week, the Japanese coastguard mobilised a fleet of some 60 ships to prevent Hong Kong and Taiwanese activists from landing on the islands, which are also claimed by Taiwan.
During his stay in Japan, Shen will also visit Okinawa, which hosts key U.S. military bases in the region and which is located close to the disputed islands.

The United States and Japan are currently reviewing defence cooperation after President Bill Clinton and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto agreed at a summit last year to redefine the bilateral security relationship for the post-Cold War era.

Current guidelines on U.S.-Japan defence cooperation laid down in 1978 only cover contingency measures in the event of a Soviet attack on Japan, and do not include any other scenario in which Japan might play a role such as a conflict on the Korean peninsula or a confrontation triggered by conflicting claims to islands in the region.
A new set of guidelines to be completed by November is expected to include Japan's role in the event of a crisis in the region, especially on the Korean peninsula.
An interim report on the new guidelines is expected to be announced next week after a meeting of defence and foreign ministry officials from Tokyo and Washington.
